questions.q: Why is disabling a compromised account and revoking its sessions a reasonable action to automate?
options: It's reversible, the correct action never changes case to case, and delaying it has a real cost
It can never be undone once it runs, so it must be automated to avoid mistakes
It requires deep investigation and business context every time it runs
Microsoft Graph does not allow this action to be performed manually
questions.explain: Reversibility and a consistently correct response, plus the real cost of delay while an attacker holds an active session, are exactly the profile of task safe to automate.

questions.q: According to the SOC Operations course's SOAR chapters referenced in this lesson, what kind of decision stays a human's job even when the response action itself is automated?
options: Deciding that the account is actually compromised in the first place
Typing the UPN into the PowerShell console
Running Connect-MgGraph to authenticate
Formatting the script's Write-Output messages
questions.explain: The judgment call of determining compromise requires context and investigation a script doesn't have — the SOAR chapters draw that same line between repeatable actions and human judgment.

questions.q: Why does the script call Revoke-MgUserSignInSession in addition to disabling the account with Update-MgUser?
options: Disabling the account alone doesn't end an already-open session, which could keep working until its access token naturally expires
Revoke-MgUserSignInSession is required before Update-MgUser will run at all
Update-MgUser only works on accounts that have no active sessions
They do the exact same thing, so calling both is redundant
questions.explain: An attacker's existing session isn't automatically killed by disabling future sign-ins — revoking the session tokens is the step that actually ends access already in progress.

questions.q: Why does the script's $UserPrincipalName parameter use [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]?
options: So the script never runs without an explicit, deliberately chosen target instead of guessing who to act on
So the script can run on every user in the tenant at once
Mandatory parameters are required by PowerShell for every script, with no real purpose
So the script skips authentication entirely
questions.explain: Making the UPN mandatory forces a deliberate choice of target every time the script runs — there is no default user it acts on automatically.

questions.q: Which of the following is explicitly NOT something this script does?
options: Decide whether the account is compromised, investigate the incident, or re-enable the account afterward
Disable the account's ability to sign in
Revoke the account's active sign-in sessions
Take a UPN as its input parameter
questions.explain: The script is deliberately scoped to just two actions, disable and revoke — deciding compromise, investigating, and re-enabling are each separate, human-decided steps.
